The following is the transcript of the interview with Rep. Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Republican Congressman Mike Lawler. He joins us today from New York. You are in this home stretch of campaigning in one of the most closely watched districts this cycle. Leader Jeffries has singled out your district as a top target for Democrats. Where do you see this headed?

REP. MIKE LAWLER: Well, I think we're going to be victorious on Tuesday night, Margaret. I've done the work, over the last four years, between my staff and I, we've closed over 10,000 constituent cases, brought back over $140 million to the district, passed over two dozen bills, 17 of which have been signed into law. Ask AOC how many she's had signed into law. The fact is, I show up, and my constituents know me. And unlike my opponent, who parachuted into this district from Virginia, I own a home here. I pay taxes. I'm raising my family here. And I think my constituents respect the fact that I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress. I'm the only sitting member of Congress endorsed by a member of the opposing party. Jared Golden endorsed my re-election just a little over a month ago, and I think people know that I've delivered for them, especially when it comes to the issue of affordability, delivering the largest tax cut in American history, including lifting the cap on salt and leading the housing bill, which will increase supply and bring down prices.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, as you just mentioned, affordability is a top issue for voters, no matter what party they are in. We are seeing the economy growing. We're still seeing consumers spend, but for the last six months, we are seeing that wages are not keeping up with inflation. Republicans campaigned on bringing prices down. Why do you deserve re-election? Why does the party deserve trust when prices have only continued to climb?

REP. LAWLER: Well, as we saw under the prior administration, inflation cumulatively rose 21%. So the baseline price of everything went up. Obviously, with the war in the Middle East, it has caused volatility in the oil markets, which- which has resulted in a- in a spike in inflation. But as you just pointed out, we saw significant growth in Q3, 3.4%. Over a million private sector jobs have been created over the past year. We are seeing purchasing power rise, but there's still work to do. And that's why I have focused extensively on what we can do to bring down prices. Number one, we did deliver the largest tax cut. Number two, we did pass the largest housing bill in 36 years to increase supply and bring down prices and increase access to capital. Before the end of this Congress--

MARGARET BRENNAN: The president didn't love that bill.

REP. LAWLER: --we will finalize a permitting- before the end of Congress, this Congress, we will finalize a permitting reform bill, which will increase domestic supply of energy, which directly impacts the prices of everything from manufacturing to transportation to groceries. And one of the problems in New York, Margaret, utilities are up 58% under Kathy Hochul because they shut down nuclear power, they ban natural gas, they blocked pipelines. We are working to rectify that. That will drive down energy prices significantly, which is critical if we're going to bring down inflation and bring down costs.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Healthcare is one of the top three issues for voters. You are one of the Republicans who tried to secure a short-term extension of those Obamacare subsidies that expired at the end of the year. In this cycle, many Democrats are promising that if they win the majority, they will restore some of those lapsed subsidies. Do you support that? Would you work with Democrats to do that?

REP. LAWLER: Oh, absolutely. Look, I've consistently been rated among the most bipartisan members of Congress. My best friend in Congress is a Democrat, Josh Gottheimer. We led that effort to negotiate a bipartisan extension of the ACA enhanced premium tax credit. Frankly, Margaret, it was Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer that rejected the bipartisan agreement. They wanted to go for a clean three-year extension with no reforms. The fact is, since the Affordable Care Act took effect, health insurance premiums are up 150% while insurance company profits are up over 2,000%. We need to fix the system.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. LAWLER: I am fully committed to addressing the healthcare costs in this country. It's the biggest driver of costs facing most Americans, and we need bipartisan solutions to actually deal with it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The OBBB, the Big Beautiful Bill, was projected to have increased the uninsured population in your state by about 860,000 people through 2034, so that tax bill also may have hurt that case. But let me ask you about something else--

REP. LAWLER: Well, respectfully, that's just- that's just not an accurate- that's just not an accurate number at all. But moreover, New York spends 80% more on Medicaid than the average of the other 49 states. Even Kathy Hochul admits they have waste, fraud, and abuse in the system with the CDPAP program that went from $10 million to $11 billion in three years.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, that's the Health Research Group KFF. Let me ask about something else. Elon Musk's Political Action Committee has put forward hundreds of thousands of dollars to support you, and your opponent, Cait Conley, has criticized you for your ties to Elon Musk. She says you're refusing to legislate on artificial intelligence or "superintelligence" to protect Elon Musk. How do you respond to that allegation?

REP. LAWLER: Well, first of all, Cait Conley is the AI candidate for the AI industry. She's the one being paid hundreds of thousands of dollars by two AI companies that she won't even tell the voters what she did to earn those contracts--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, what does Elon Musk expect for that?

REP. LAWLER: --secondarily, I'm leading on this issue- second, wait a minute. Well, first of all, it's an outside group, so I've had no communication with anybody that's spending in this race. Second of all, I'm the one leading on these issues with Josh Gottheimer, the Stop Rogue AI Act to set national standards with respect to these rogue agents and bots, and secondarily for the frontier models to require mandatory testing. Third, Cait Conley has violated federal election law by setting up a JFC with the House Super PAC, the House Democrat Super PAC, and she is spending out of that on campaign ads, millions of dollars. And lastly, Margaret, in the last week, a Democrat Super PAC popped up. They have not filed with the FEC in clear violation of election law, spending millions of dollars saying that I support amnesty for criminal illegal aliens. It is a straight-up lie--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Who is behind that?

REP. LAWLER: --they are trying to drive down Republican turnout. These are Democrats supporting this. They did this two years ago, and they're doing it again. American Forge Group. This is a straight-up fraud perpetrated on the voters, like they're doing in Alaska.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

REP. LAWLER: And frankly, the FBI and the Department of Justice have informed us that they are investigating it--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

REP. LAWLER: --and it should be investigated.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Alright.

REP. LAWLER: They are violating election law, so people should be focused--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REP. LAWLER: --very clearly on what is actually happening in our elections.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes, we did ask the Conley campaign about that, and they told CBS they had nothing to do with the mailers being sent out. But we will ask the Justice Department as well. Thank you, Congressman Lawler.

REP. LAWLER: And they didn't condemn it either. Yep. Thank you.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will be watching your race, sir. Back in a moment.

France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe

toggle caption i Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.

Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

Sponsor Message

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

The marchers' grievances are diverse.

Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Sponsor Message

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.

Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.

Police impose curfew and other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.

Sponsor Message

In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.

Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

Thousands of students and supporters in Serbia have marked two years since a deadly train station disaster

Serbia marks the second anniversary of a train station tragedy that fueled student protests

A rose is placed outside the train station in Novi Sad, Serbia, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, on the second anniversary of the canopy collapse disaster that killed 16 people. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic)

A rose is placed outside the train station in Novi Sad, Serbia, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, on the second anniversary of the canopy collapse disaster that killed 16 people. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic)

A rose is placed outside the train station in Novi Sad, Serbia, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, on the second anniversary of the canopy collapse disaster that killed 16 people. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic)

A rose is placed outside the train station in Novi Sad, Serbia, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, on the second anniversary of the canopy collapse disaster that killed 16 people. (AP Photo/Darko Vojinovic)

NOVI SAD, Serbia -- A week after a student movement toppled Serbia's strongman Aleksandar Vucic in an election, thousands of students and their supporters on Sunday marked two years since a deadly train station disaster that gave birth to their anti-corruption campaign.

The demand for accountability over the Nov. 1, 2024 collapse of a concrete canopy at the station in the northern city of Novi Sad that killed 16 people launched two years of student-led protests that eventually brought about the stunning defeat of Vucic’s right-wing government at last week's parliamentary elections.

In steady rain and silence, thousands marched in Novi Sad on Sunday in a gesture of respect for the victims. Unlike a year ago, when huge crowds gathered for the first anniversary of the tragedy, participants this year said they now have hope that those responsible for the disaster will be punished.

The students brought 16 wreaths and 16 red hearts — one for each victim — outside the station building. The inscribed names of the victims included children. People cried as they laid down flowers and lit candles. A moment of silence was held.

Many in Serbia believe that the concrete canopy crashed because of flawed renovation work caused by corruption and negligence that prevailed in major state infrastructure projects championed by Vucic's government.

The station renovation was part of a bigger railway reconstruction project with China and neighboring Hungary. Vucic and his ally, former right-wing Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban together toured the renewed Novi Sad station back in 2022.

“It was a murder and a murder demands accountability and justice,” a student said in a speech Sunday, promising that Serbia’s young people will build a more just society in the future. “We will not forget them (victims).”

Since the election in which the Students’ List defeated Vucic’s long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, last Sunday, the students have demanded a review of high-profile investigations, including the probe into the canopy collapse. Previously, 13 people had been charged, including a government minister, but no trial was held as the probe stalled.

The head of the European Union mission in Serbia, Andreas von Beckerath, wrote on X that the canopy collapse “shook Serbia to its core and moved citizens across the country to demand transparency and accountability.”

“May their memory keep inspiring a Serbia built on solidarity, public trust and rule of law," he added.

Also Sunday, prosecutors ordered a 48-hour detention of Marko Kricak, Vucic's chief of criminal police. Another senior officer was detained along with Kricak, both on suspicion of abuse of office in connection with a murder investigation.

Kricak was accused of orchestrating violence during the student protests, and of personally threatening a female student with rape, allegations that he has denied.

After it took office 14 years ago, Vucic's SNS party gradually took control of all state institutions. The students' movement has promised to restore the rule of law and democracy, and root out rampant graft that they say flourished under Vucic.

On Nov. 1, 2024, the huge concrete construction at the outer front wall of the Novi Sad station crashed without warning at 11:52 a.m., crushing people underneath as they were waiting for trains on a sunny autumn day.

Fourteen people died at the scene, and two died later. A young woman survived with life-changing injuries.

Authorities first said that the canopy had not been renovated at all, and promised an investigation. But protests started almost immediately with people blocking traffic every day across the country at the exact time of the collapse and demanding justice.

Some of the student-led rallies held in the last two years were among the biggest anti-government protests in Serbia's history.

And unlike last year when Vucic was in power, Sunday's anniversary memorial was broadcast by state RTS television, following resignations among officials at the TV station in the post-election week.

Commemoration ceremonies were also held in other cities and towns throughout Serbia.

An independent investigation by a group of experts into the canopy collapse found the renovation work had been rushed under political orders. The experts' report alleged a “systematic degradation of construction standards” and said that the "state of Serbia violated its citizens' right to life.”

Oyster stocks have plunged in the Chesapeake. This resident wants to bring them back

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

John Consoli stands on the edge of his pier, which juts out from the southern tip of Maryland's Kent Island and into the Chesapeake Bay. He leans over and hoists a mesh the size and shape of a pillowcase out of the water.

It's packed with oysters. He manages to get it onto the pier. "These are brand new oysters from this year," he says. "When I got them, they weighed nothing. And this is just three months of growth. The net is chock full, I can hardly pull it up."

Once he catches his breath, Consoli marvels at these molluscs. "I think I'm more enthusiastic about something that's like a rock than anybody else could possibly be," he says with a big grin. "I really can't think of many more creatures that do the good that oysters do."

Sponsor Message

Oysters underpin the Chesapeake's coastal and estuarine ecosystem. Each adult filters up to 50 gallons of water a day. Cleaner water leads to a healthier bay and more sea grass. "That helps crabs and other organisms," says Consoli.

Plus, oyster shells are a habitat unto themselves. "Because of all the nooks and crannies," he explains, "a lot of small fish and crabs live and eat amongst them and hide, so it creates a biodiverse environment. I even found a seahorse, which was incredible. I've never seen a seahorse in my life!"

Robots scanning for oysters

Oyster reefs used to abound in the Chesapeake, but overharvesting decimated their ranks — by over 99% by 2011, according to one estimate. This monumental shift in the bay contributed to poorer water quality and less habitat for other species.

Oyster farming in the Chesapeake has expanded in recent years, despite environmental and disease challenges, says Ryan Carnegie, a biologist at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. He adds that wild oysters have also made a partial comeback, helped by better management and investments in restoration. But, says Elizabeth North, a fisheries oceanographer at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, "current oyster populations are likely still a fraction of these historic populations."

Consoli's goal, therefore, is to be a caretaker of sorts, stocking the bay with ever more oysters and looking after their wellbeing. He floats them just below the surface where he says the nutrients are concentrated to help them grow quickly. And although his oysters aren't intended for eating, a cleaner bay does mean better habitat for those that are harvested commercially.

Sponsor Message

Consoli came to oyster conservation in a roundabout way: He's a professional photographer at the University of Maryland and he was doing a shoot involving the campus's oyster research — namely, efforts to understand and support oyster reefs.

"Seeing great minds coming together to solve problems showed to me that there's a real need here," he says.

Miao Yu is one of the great minds who inspired Consoli that day. She's a mechanical engineer at the University of Maryland who has observed that despite the recent, modest gains in oyster abundance, farmers continue to face two daunting tasks — both of which are stymied by the bay's murky waters.

The first is knowing where to plant the babies. A young oyster needs to settle upon a hard substrate. But finding that ideal spot is much easier said than done. "Sometimes it's dropped into [the] mud," she explains — where the young oyster suffocates and dies.

The second task involves figuring out where and when to harvest the adult oysters. "It's the biggest challenge," she says. "We cannot see like a couple feet down there."

This means that the recovery of oysters, often via dredging, tends to be inefficient, and even damaging: It can harm the seabed or pull up oysters that aren't yet ready for harvest.

The fishermen, she says, "don't have a whole picture of what's going on. So our goal is to transform that guesswork into precision."

Yu is trying to do that with the help of robots. She and her team frequently work inside the Neutral Buoyancy Research Facility on campus, which houses a giant cylindrical tank.

toggle caption i Ari Daniel/NPR

On a recent fall morning, one of Yu's PhD students, Michael Xu, uses a joystick to steer a raft-like robot called Oysterbot. Oysterbot, which the team built in-house, consists of a collection of electronics and cables atop a couple of pontoons. A sonar is mounted below.

Sponsor Message

"We're able to do a large-range scan to get a general view of what's going on down there," says Xu.

The team can also deploy a smaller off-the-shelf robot known as the BlueROV to examine something underwater more closely through a live video feed. Together, the two robots paint a portrait of the seabed.

The lab then uses AI to stitch the visuals together and analyze them "to determine if the oysters are present, how many of them are alive or dead, and how big they are," says Xu.

They're still refining the algorithms, but Yu says the eventual goal is "to turn that sonar image map into an oyster information map." In other words, she wants to provide farmers with actionable intelligence to know when and where to plant and harvest their oysters.

Beyond the Chesapeake, her team has conducted field work along the shoreline of Washington state and the Gulf coast. Yu is hoping that within a decade, the technology could be modified and scaled to coastlines nationwide, "so that we can help the oysters for the entire United States."

Peer to Pier

This interest in aiding oysters elsewhere appeals to Consoli as well. Ever since he got hooked, he can't help but spread the good word to a growing number of neighbors with access to the bay.

"Every time I meet a new person, I ask them, 'Hey, do you like oysters?" he says. "And even if they say no, I say, 'Well, somebody in your family likes oysters. Have to be! You have a brother, uncle, a brother-in-law.'" Once he establishes such a connection, he says to them, "Hey, can you grow them? It's not that hard."

And most of the time, Consoli finds that people are quite receptive. That includes a couple of octogenarian neighbors of his on Kent Island.

Sponsor Message

"I really am impressed that the oysters clean the bay," says Earl Collins.

On one occasion, Ann Ziegler, who lives a couple doors down from Consoli, says she pulled her oysters out of the water with her family to eat them raw. "And then, at Thanksgiving, since no one had died, we ate them again," she says.

Consoli has also met new neighbors through this work, like John Patrick. "It's just amazing the amount of marine life that I've seen around the pier since I've had these oysters in the water," he says. "I had croaker, crabs and eels in here this morning."

Even Consoli's dental hygienist has gotten involved.

Perhaps most ambitiously, Consoli worked with a local restaurant called Libbey's Coastal Kitchen in August to place a million baby oysters around their dock pilings.

"We had eight people in wetsuits and life jackets," he says. "There were jellyfish everywhere. It was probably the most difficult installation we could ever do."

Restaurant operator Andrew Westlin says he was instantly attracted to the idea.

"This was a no-brainer for us, honestly," he says. "We felt that this was a cool way for us to give back and just be part of the community." Soon, there will be a sign next to the pier explaining the oyster project to any restaurant customers and passersby.

Consoli's wife, Kathy, says all this oyster work is "the most hardworking hobby there is. I call him now the Pied Piper of oysters because I think he's up to 80 people possibly."

She's right. Consoli calls it his Peer to Pier Network.

"We're really just trying to make sure that we can restore as much as we can to the bay," he says, "whether that's with robots or other techniques… It teaches me just how something that seems so insignificant can make a difference."

Luigi Mangione appears at a hearing in Manhattan Criminal Court in New York, May 18, 2026.

Luigi Mangione appears at a hearing in Manhattan Criminal Court in New York, May 18, 2026.

Luigi Mangione appears at a hearing in Manhattan Criminal Court in New York, May 18, 2026.

Luigi Mangione's attorneys are pushing for a double jeopardy claim in his state trial for the 2024 shooting of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, according to a court filing submitted Friday.

Mangione pleaded guilty to stalking charges in federal court in August when he admitted to traveling to New York with the intent to kill Thompson and shooting him outside the Midtown Hilton.

Luigi Mangione attends a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan Criminal Court, in New York City, August 11, 2026. David Dee Delgado/Reuters, FILE

His attorneys argued that the guilty plea means Mangione has been sufficiently prosecuted for killing the CEO and putting him on trial in state court for murder would amount to double jeopardy.

"There are no cases where the identical conduct -- the same victim, the same gun, the same actions by the defendant, the same place and the same time -- that was prosecuted by federal authorities was then also prosecuted by state authorities," defense attorney Karen Agnifilo wrote in the filing.

Agnifilo previously told reporters New York law "does not permit a person to be prosecuted and punished twice for the exact same crime under a statute that governs successive prosecutions."

The Manhattan District Attorney's office is pushing to put Mangione on trial in state court, arguing the deal offense of stalking and the state charge of murder address different misconduct. The new defense filing said the "core misconduct" is effectively the same.

"Yes, stalking can also, in some circumstances, apply to conduct different and less extreme than intending to kill someone. But this has nothing to do with whether it also applies to intentional killing," the defense filing said.

The Manhattan DA's office didn't immediately comment on the filing.

Luigi Mangione appears for a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan Criminal Court in New York City, June 17, 2026. Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo, FILE

Mangione is slated to be sentenced for his federal charges in December.

That same month, Judge Gregory Carro will hear oral arguments on a defense motion to dismiss the state murder indictment.

https://www.cbsnews.com/news/france-prot.text:
French police fired tear gas and clashed with some protesters on Saturday as thousands marched across France again in largely peaceful demonstrations against soaring living costs and police violence.

Police said about 70,000 people demonstrated in Paris alone. France's interior ministry said about 320,000 people rallied nationwide.

In the southern port city of Marseille, demonstrators clashed with police. In Lyon, France's third-largest city, people threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire tear gas, according to a journalist at the scene. In the southern city of Toulouse, police used water cannon against an unauthorized protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators, some of them in costume.

Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night, The Associated Press reported. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays.

A protester waves a French flag while taking part in a demonstration in Lyon, France, on Oct. 31, 2026. Jeff Pachoud /AFP via Getty Images

In Paris, thousands of people, some wearing costumes ranging from Spider-Man to Frankenstein, walked through eastern Paris as a helicopter circled overhead. Placards read: "No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak" and "Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween." Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has accused French President Emmanuel Macron's government of "taking an increasingly authoritarian turn," joined the march.

"We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students' demands, yes to giving citizens a voice," Camille Guerin, 31, said in the western city of Nantes.

In the northern French city of Lille, 47-year-old Aurelie Herrmann danced at the protest.

"I dance because on television they only show damage and destruction, whereas you can perfectly well demonstrate in good spirits," she said.

Demonstrators take part in a protest in Paris, France on Oct. 31, 2026. Ibrahim Ezzat/Anadolu via Getty Images

An aide to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday that police had prepared for street violence on a scale "comparable" to the unrest two weeks ago, when shops were looted and public buildings set ablaze. Nunez said authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening that urged protesters to spark a "revolution."

Some shopkeepers again prepared by barricading their businesses.

"Everyone is staying home. No one is going to come and buy anything," said Wael Boubaker, a cafe employee in eastern Paris, as he covered a storefront with plywood panels.

Alain Di Crescenzo, president of France's chamber of commerce, said business owners were worried.

"Shopkeepers can't wait for Saturday to be over," Di Crescenzo told broadcaster France Inter.

Protests come as elections near

The demonstrations come in a febrile political climate, with presidential elections less than six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading the polls.

The protest movement, bringing together activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on the rising cost of living, inequality, and deteriorating learning conditions.

French Republican Security Corps police officers stand during demonstrations in Marseille, France on Oct. 31, 2026. Miguel Medina / AFP via Getty Images

Following a security clampdown and serious injuries to some protesters, the movement broadened its demands to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest. This week, student protesters complained that the police did not authorize a march through the center of the French capital, and vowed to stage new blockades of high schools and universities next week.

With the eurozone's second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in its debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.

Similar youth-led demonstrations have been seen across Europe in recent weeks. Thousands of young Germans took to the streets nationwide on Saturday.

Why so many horror movies have Catholic themes

toggle caption i Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images

(NPR) Think of some of the most iconic scenes in classics of the horror genre:

Priests gathered around a possessed child in The Exorcist.

The chanting of the neighborhood coven in Rosemary's Baby.

The priest warning Damien's father in The Omen.

Notice a theme?

Horror villains and monsters show up in all shapes and sizes, but when religion shows up, it is usually Catholicism.

In Hollywood, it's the faith often featured for its mysterious conclaves and Gothic churches, depicting the white clerical collar up against the ultimate prince of darkness.

"When a vampire is at your door or your child is possessed, you don't call for a Methodist," said Matthew J. Cressler, the co-author of the new book Body and Blood: Catholic Horror in America, along with Jack Lee Downey, Kathleen Holscher and Michael Pasquier.

Sponsor Message

"God love the Unitarians, but you don't ask for your Unitarian minister. You grab your rosary beads, your St. Christopher medal, your holy water, your priest."

toggle caption i Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images

Cressler said Catholicism also has theological themes that work with the genre.

"Catholics have long had a sense that when one suffers, one is bearing the cross of Christ. And that in suffering, one is drawn closer to Christ," he said.

Aislinn Clarke said having an Irish Catholic childhood was the perfect preparation to become a horror film director. She wrote and directed the 2024 horror movie Fréwaka.

"I remember reading a book about the lives of the saints, which my parents probably thought was a very wholesome thing for a child to read," said Clarke.

"But there was a lot of stuff about, like, St. Lucia plucked out her eyeballs, and another saint cut off her breasts. And everybody's wearing hair shirts and thorns and flagellating."

Of course, horror movies take these ideas and ratchet them up to 11, Cressler said.

He argued that Catholic themes, like venerating the remains of the beloved dead, can show up in movies that are not even overtly Catholic. For example, keeping the mummified corpse of your mother in the basement of the house next to your roadside motel, as Norman Bates does in Psycho.

toggle caption i Giuseppe Anastasi/AP

Beyond the fictionalized depictions, it is a faith that can take spiritual warfare fairly literally. The Rev. Aaron Williams, a pastor at the Basilica of Saint Mary in Natchez, Mississippi, consulted on the 2025 horror film The Ritual.

Sponsor Message

Williams said that while most people are far more likely to fall into sin through temptation rather than possession, "we do come in contact with the occult and the enemy and his minions, the demons."

Though the average Catholic may not hold these views, the church still performs the rite of exorcism. And the Catholic Church positions its clergy to deal with ultimate evil by imbuing them with ultimate good.

"A priest … through ordination, he's sacramentally received a character that allows him to act with the authority of Christ," Williams said.

Some films use that heightened authority to save characters from the demonic. And some use horror to point out broken elements in the church itself. Clarke discussed a scene from her 2018 film, The Devil's Doorway, in which nuns sing hymns to Christ and perform a brutal symphysiotomy procedure while ignoring the suffering of the young woman giving birth in front of them.

It was a nod to the confinement of women in Magdalene laundries, asylums run by Protestants and Catholics between the 18th and 20th centuries.

"There are things flying around, and crosses going upside down, and we have some stuff like that," Clarke said. "But the most horrific scene in the movie from the script stage for me was always going to be this birth sequence."

Catholic symbols and songs show up in horror so much so that Cressler said it can influence how we see the church itself.

"If you walk into a room that's got too many candles and too many crosses and too many statues, you know you're in trouble," he said.

But Cressler said that also goes for the tropes of Catholic grace and redemption. Horror films bring our fears out into the open. And in seeing them, we can, in some ways, defeat our monsters — at least until they're resurrected for the sequel.

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

This Halloween marks 100 years since legendary magician Harry Houdini died in Detroit, but his spirit still haunts the Motor City, as Quinn Klinefelter reports from Detroit member station WDET.

QUINN KLINEFELTER, BYLINE: Harry Houdini played Detroit 19 times during his career, escaping initial obscurity the way he did handcuffs and straitjackets, and repeatedly defying death. By 1914, Houdini had unveiled his ultimate stunt.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

HARRY HOUDINI: Ladies and gentlemen, my latest invention, the water torture cell.

KLINEFELTER: The water torture cell was a coffin-sized box filled with water. Houdini was lowered into it upside down, and even stage assistant, Dorothy Young, who'd seen the stunt many times, had goosebumps.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

DOROTHY YOUNG: Mrs. H always stood in the wing because they had a secret code in case he couldn't get out.

KLINEFELTER: Young was the last surviving person to work with Houdini before she, too, died in 2011. A few years before, in an interview, Young recalled how the magician said he could withstand any punch to his muscular stomach, but a college wrestler punched him several times before he could tighten his midsection.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

YOUNG: One time he showed me that, you know, he had a way of doing it, and to think those boys didn't give him a chance to get himself protected.

KLINEFELTER: It was 1926. Houdini was enroute to Detroit for a series of shows. Detroit Historical Museum curator Jeremy Dimick says Houdini arrived weak and running a high fever but under financial pressure to fulfill his contract.

JEREMY DIMICK: He doesn't have the strength to put his makeup on before the show. And then he has to be literally carried from the Garrick Theater back to his hotel. And when he gets to Grace Hospital, he is evaluated, and they realize that he's ruptured his appendix.

KLINEFELTER: Several days and two surgeries later, Houdini breathed his last. His wife, Bess Houdini, searched for his ghost for years, holding seance after seance, even though the magician himself spent his final years exposing psychics he felt preyed on the bereaved. But after a decade, Bess Houdini finally said good night to Harry.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

BESS HOUDINI: And do you remember what he always said about these things? That it was impossible for the dead to return. This proves he was right. For if it would have been possible, I would have had some sign from him in the past 10 years.

KLINEFELTER: That did not stop others from trying to contact the Great Houdini, sometimes even incorporating old pieces of his stage act.

(SOUNDBITE OF MILK CAN BANGING)

JOHN SHERWOOD: That is the Houdini milk can. Houdini would jump into this while it was filled with warm water, and he would be locked inside with six Mastodon locks...

(SOUNDBITE OF LOCKS RATTLING)

SHERWOOD: ...Right here.

KLINEFELTER: John Sherwood is with the American Museum of Magic, about a hundred miles west of Detroit. He's been part of several past seances.

SHERWOOD: Wanted to lure him in by essentially appealing to Houdini's Jewish heritage by placing a lox and bagel sandwich into the milk can and invite Houdini's spirit to take a bite out of it.

KLINEFELTER: Now Sherwood is orchestrating another attempt. He says a centennial of Houdini's death might resonate with his sense of showmanship.

SHERWOOD: I've always said that the greatest publicity stunt that Harry Houdini ever pulled off was dying on Halloween. Because after that, the mythology about him grew by leaps and bounds.

KLINEFELTER: It still conjures conspiracy theories. Was Houdini's death certificate altered? Was he assassinated by angry psychics? In some ways, Houdini's death mirrors the stunts he performed in life - shrouded in mystery.

For NPR News, I'm Quinn Klinefelter in Detroit.

ANCHORAGE, Alaska -- The FBI has begun reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation of the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.

Agents have contacted donors in at least two remote communities in Alaska and a couple in Massachusetts . An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. The agent left a business card for Charles Flint, who told The Associated Press he has known Dan J. Sullivan for years as a respected teacher and musician.

The FBI visits came after federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over the candidate. The U.S. Department of Justice also pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion.

Flint contributed $500 over the summer to what he considered a long-shot campaign, saying he knew Dan J. Sullivan would have expenses and respected him for “throwing his hat in the ring.” Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been “misled” about which candidate he was supporting.

“I don’t feel like I’ve been misled at all,” Flint, who has been out of town, told the AP in a telephone interview, adding he had no intention of calling the agent but would “let him waste his time trying to track me down.”

“I don’t think there’s any confusion,” he said, adding he intends to rank Democrat Mary Peltola first on his ballot, followed by Dan J. Sullivan. “Everybody knows who the incumbent is.”

President Donald Trump was asked about the case on Saturday night, during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate, and called it “voter fraud at the highest level.” He also suggested that Dan J. Sullivan had gone into hiding: “Nobody can find him now, so he knows he’s guilty.”

The president also suggested, without providing details, that top Democratic leaders outside the state could have been involved, and that they should be prosecuted.

Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage the federal investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”

Two different FBI agents were dispatched to Sitka to conduct a brief interview at the doorstep of another donor. That donor, who asked that their name not be published given the ongoing investigation, said the agents asked whether the contribution had been made to the Sullivan the donor intended. The conversation lasted about five minutes, the donor told the AP.

The donor said the agents were “scrupulously polite” and emphasized that the conversation was entirely voluntary.

Yet another donor, Pat Campbell, of Groton, Massachusetts, said a couple of FBI agents came to her door Friday and spoke with her husband.

“They said they were from the FBI and investigating fraud in election contributions,” Campbell wrote in a text message to AP. “No, we had not been defrauded. We knew to whom we had contributed.”

The developments come just days before Tuesday’s ranked choice general election in a potentially pivotal race in which Peltola, a former congresswoman, is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

At a campaign rally in Anchorage on Friday, Peltola again denied involvement in any plan to place candidates on the ballot to detract from the incumbent senator.

She said she was “deeply offended” by the allegations, which she called “garbage” and part of a “smear campaign” to suppress turnout on the eve of the election.

“I know I can beat Dan Sullivan. I do not need any help winning this race,” she told a small group of campaign volunteers at an Anchorage aviation museum. ___ Mustian reported from New York. Associated Press writer Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, contributed to this report.

https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-602.title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-602.text:
'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.

When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

Sponsor Message

The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.

Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists.

The White House did not immediately react publicly to Saturday's dismissal or respond to an AP request for comment.

Trump called the reporting 'malicious'

The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.

The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper.

Sponsor Message

Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory."

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.

Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.

The lawsuit was dismissed once, then refiled

Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.

In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.

"The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote. "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."

The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, "Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."

Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

https://www.cbsnews.com/news/daylight-sa.authors: Alex, Senior Editor, Alex Sundis A Senior Editor At Cbsnews.Com. In Addition To Editing Content, Alex Also Covers Breaking News, Writing About Crime, Severe Weather As Well As Everything Multistate Lottery Jackpots To The July Fourth Hot Dog Eating Contest., Read Full Bio
https://www.cbsnews.com/news/daylight-sa.text:
Millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight saving ended for 2026. Most of the U.S. "fell back" an hour when the clocks changed at 2 a.m. on Sunday.

Here's what to know about what's formally known as daylight saving time as it ended for the year:

What is daylight saving time, and why do we have it?

Daylight saving time is the period during the year, from March to early November, when the majority of the U.S. operates one hour ahead of standard time.

The move effectively "saves" an hour of daylight from the morning and adds it to the evening during the spring and summer months when the days are the longest. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.

For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun rose at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.

The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service. After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.

During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. These experiments didn't last long.

After the war, the U.S. let states and municipalities decide for themselves if they wanted to keep daylight saving time and when to observe it. (Congress didn't establish a uniform start and end for the time change until 1966.) In the 1970s, continuous daylight saving time was stopped before reaching the 10-month mark.

Will the U.S. move to year-round daylight saving time?

Earlier this year, legislation to once again make daylight saving time last all year long cleared a major hurdle in Congress. The bill, called the Sunshine Protection Act, passed the House in July and went to the Senate. The legislation would also let states opt out of daylight saving time altogether before the law takes effect.

President Trump, who supports the bill, accused a fellow Republican, Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, of holding up the legislation. Mr. Trump even posted to social media what he said was Cotton's cellphone number and urged people to call the senator to express their support for the measure.

In response, Cotton noted Congress has tried permanent daylight saving time before, only to go back to the twice-yearly time change "once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter."

There is a ticking clock for the Senate to take action on the bill. The legislation and any other bills awaiting approval in Congress are set to expire in early January when the new class of lawmakers elected in Tuesday's midterm elections takes office.

If the bill does die, the effort to change daylight saving time will have to start over and be approved by the House and the Senate before it can go to the president.

Did the time change today?

Yes, the time changed at 2 a.m. local time Sunday.

For 2026, the end of daylight saving time came during the overnight hours after Halloween, giving revelers an extra hour of enjoying late-night costume parties — or an extra hour of sleep to recover from their fun.

But for parents of young children, the time change may have been more of a trick and less of a treat, potentially disrupting their kids' sleep schedules until they adjust.

What day and time did daylight saving time end in November 2026?

Daylight saving time officially ended at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, Nov. 1.

Americans have been "falling back" on the first Sunday of November since 2007, when the most recent changes to daylight saving time took effect. A 2005 law moved the end date from the last Sunday of October.

Do we lose or gain an hour when daylight saving time ended?

Most Americans gained an hour when daylight saving time ended, making up for the hour they lost when the clocks "sprang forward" in March.

When will daylight saving time start again in 2027?

Daylight saving time is set to begin in 2027 on Sunday, March 14, at 2 a.m. local time. The time change starts on the second Sunday of March, which falls on such a late date next year because the month starts on a Monday. In 2026, daylight saving time started on March 8.

The start date was also changed in 2007 to extend the length of daylight saving time, which previously began on the first Sunday of April.

Which states don't do daylight saving time?

Daylight saving time is observed in every state except for Hawaii and most of Arizona. The Navajo Nation, which is located in part of Arizona, observes the time change to stay on the same time as their communities in the neighboring states of New Mexico and Utah, according to the tribe.

The U.S. territories of American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands also don't observe daylight saving time.

Will my phone change for daylight saving time automatically?

Phones should change overnight to display the correct time if they're set to update automatically.

Apple, Google and Samsung have support pages with instructions for changing the clocks on their devices. Carriers like Simple Mobile and Straight Talk have also posted steps online for checking the settings on other phones.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

It is a pretty good time to be a witch in Salem, Massachusetts, certainly compared to 1692, when dozens of witchcraft claims led to 19 public executions plus other deaths in prison. This was, of course, the Salem witch trials. Over 300 years later, the story is why a different of mass hysteria takes over Salem every fall. The small city just north of Boston has become enormously popular for Halloween tourists in October. Reporter Megan Johnson has written about what that is like for boston.com and is with us now. Welcome.

MEGAN JOHNSON: Hi.

DETROW: Tell me what the draw is. I mean, it makes sense. This historic town tied to witch trials - makes sense that it would be a Halloween destination. But, like, what is there to do? Say you're thinking of driving up to Salem to check it out in October. What's available?

JOHNSON: There is so much to do. Besides the fact that it is just an absolutely stunning town that is the epitome of autumn when the weather changes, people love the historic aspect, so they want to go to the Salem Witch Museum, the House of Seven Gables, the nun on stilts, which is one of the very common buskers on the street. There's people in costume all the time. It's a big bachelorette trip draw.

DETROW: Has all of this grown in recent years? Like, and is there...

JOHNSON: Absolutely.

DETROW: ...A particular reason for that?

JOHNSON: So it has grown tremendously in recent years, pretty across the board, every resident has said. And a lot of them really attribute that to social media - Instagram, social media influencers who descend upon the city and want to caption amazing content. And because there's so much of that content out there, that brings such a draw of visitors who see it and want to participate in it, too.

DETROW: So let's set the scene. It's about 45,000 people live in Salem, and - what? - a million people visit in October. What is that like on a fall Saturday?

JOHNSON: The No. 1 complaint that people have is that it's nonstop traffic, and there's nowhere to park, and that comes from residents and visitors. But there's also just a constant onslaught of people in the streets, which often get shut down as an attempt to get rid of some of the traffic. But moving around, navigating the streets is pretty crazy.

DETROW: You wrote about a bunch of different examples of funny run-ins between residents and Halloween tourists. Can you tell us a couple of them?

JOHNSON: Yes. They really range from the overwhelmingly positive - people who have met just wonderful people, like the World Cup visitors from Scotland. They just thought they were absolutely wonderful. But then the people who have visitors throwing bottles in their yards, busting up their pumpkins, nonstop tours walking through their streets maybe three times an hour. And the kind of most unusual thing is that a lot of tourists don't seem to realize that there are actual residents who are living there. So it kind of Disney-fies the experience for many of them. They just see it as kind of a play town when really there's people behind those doors that they're accidentally walking into.

DETROW: What is your best suggestion for somebody who, on one hand, says, this sounds great, and on the other hand, says, I don't want to make it worse for these poor people who live in Salem? Like, how can you enjoy the experience without being that person?

JOHNSON: They really want to encourage whatever people can do to not drive into the city. Because there's so little parking for residents already, there's already so little parking for visitors, as well. The Salem commuter rail on the MBTA is very already very filled, so a lot of people are on there. But one of the best recommendations that I got from a city counselor was, take an Uber, have it drop you off on the outskirts of the city, and you can walk in and not have to worry about anything, including the high price of parking.

JOHNSON: Thank you so much.

Los Angeles leaders are speaking out after video captured the moments when what appeared to be a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pointed a gun at a bystander as a different man was detained in North Hollywood on Friday.

The cell phone footage shows a man being taken away by several masked agents just seconds before the bystander, who was walking two dogs, appeared to pick something up off the ground. He was then rushed by two agents, one of whom pushed the man into some bushes while holding what looked to be a handgun. The bystander tossed the item almost instantly, at which point the agent backed away.

As the video continues, the dog walker can be heard yelling at the officers before one approached him again, holding what witnesses said was pepper spray, causing him to run down the street. As he's running, he can again be seen bending down to pick something up, which he tosses further down the street. It's unclear what the object was.

In the video, the agents are seen wearing vests that say "ICE Police" while dragging the detained man towards an unmarked SUV parked in the street.

It happened at around 8:30 a.m. near the Ivy Apartments on Vineland Place and Otsego Street. Damari Butler, who lives in the area, said he watched the entire ordeal.

"He draws his gun and puts it right in the guy's face," Butler said. "Which was insane. At that moment, I realized how real this was, because, respectfully, I didn't know what was about to happen to that guy."

In a statement provided to CBS LA Saturday on the incident, DHS said agents arrested Angel Luis Gonzalez Lobo from Venezuela during a targeted operation.

"He was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge after failing to show up for his court date. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings and will receive due process," DHS said in its statement.

DHS also addressed the incident with the bystander, claiming he was armed with pepper spray, creating "a moment of chaos."

"These actions by these individuals created an unnecessarily dangerous, and precarious environment for federal law enforcement as they endeavored to carry out their lawful duties and effect an arrest," DHS said.

Several L.A. city leaders also addressed the incident Friday night after the video began to gain traction on social media.

"It is alarming to see the images and reports coming out of North Hollywood this morning," said Mayor Karen Bass in a statement. "Every Angeleno deserves to feel safe in their own community. No one should have to live in fear because of where they come from, what language they speak, or how they look."

Congresswoman Luz Rivas, who represents the area, called the video "horrifying."

"ICE is violating the fundamental rights and safety of individuals across the San Fernando Valley to carry out Donald Trump's anti-immigrant agenda," Rivas said in a statement. "Families are being ripped apart and hardworking residents are being terrorized on their own streets by masked thugs. ICE needs to get out of L.A. and it must be abolished for good."

Mayoral candidate and Los Angeles City Councilwoman Nithya Raman also shared her "outrage" on social media.

"LA is not a playground for the Trump regime's inhumane operations, and Angelenos should not have to live in fear of going to work, taking their kids to school, or living their life," Raman's statement said.

DeMonica Amerson's diagnosis of multiple sclerosis in 2001 had been a shock. No one in her family had ever had the autoimmune condition, and it had been difficult to diagnose. Doctors had first thought she had optic neuritis because her symptoms were in her eyes. Then they suspected lupus. After a spinal tap, she was diagnosed with MS.

At the time, Amerson had never heard about the condition. She had just graduated from college and expected to be in the prime of her life. Instead, she had to give herself daily shots to treat the condition.

"I was mad, I was hurt, I was nervous, confused, all the things," said Amerson.

But over the years, her perspective changed. As MS treatment evolved, she moved from daily shots to a monthly infusion. A port was placed in her chest to make the medication easier to deliver. She engaged in advocacy and fundraising through the MS National Foundation. She got married and welcomed two daughters, and worked as a school administrator. Even as her condition threw curveballs, including the occasional relapse, she "just kept going." Amerson attributed those relapses to the progressive nature of MS. Her doctors never suggested otherwise.

DeMonica Amerson receives treatment through a chest port. DeMonica Amerson

Then, in 2019, she had a significant flare. She was lethargic, and her legs were numb. Amerson immediately went to the hospital, missing her daughter's birthday party. In the ER, she began to feel pressure in her eyes and began vomiting. An on-call neurologist examined her and ran a specialized blood test. Eventually, Amerson's condition stabilized, and she was discharged. A few days after returning home, she received a call from the neurologist. The doctor believed she had a rare autoimmune disorder and recommended she see her neurologist. Amerson was horrified to receive that diagnosis on top of her MS. When she saw her neurologist, he sent her to a specialist.

Follow-up testing by the specialist revealed something shocking: Amerson had never had multiple sclerosis at all.

The risk of MS misdiagnosis

Dr. Robert Bermel, the director of the Mellen Center for MS at Cleveland Clinic, told CBS News earlier in October that large studies looking at the risk of MS misdiagnosis have found that between 15% and 20% of patients diagnosed with multiple sclerosis are eventually found to not have the condition.

The topic burst into the mainstream earlier this month, when actor Christina Applegate announced on her MeSsy podcast that she had been incorrectly diagnosed with MS for nearly five years. Applegate, who uses mobility aids to walk, said doctors are still not sure what's causing her symptoms.

Dr. Josef Gutman, the director of NYU Langone's Long Island Comprehensive MS Care Center, previously told CBS News that the wide spectrum of symptoms that can be attributed to multiple sclerosis makes the condition difficult to diagnose. Both Bermel and Gutman said there are a number of autoimmune diseases that can mimic MS. A misdiagnosis is usually found when someone's symptoms do not respond to MS treatment, spurring more specialized tests.

Christina Applegate onstage at the 75th Primetime Emmy Awards on January 15, 2024. Christopher Polk/Variety via Getty Images

Typically, a misdiagnosis occurs because abnormalities on a brain scan are misinterpreted, Bermel said. New diagnostic criteria, published in 2025, are trying to reduce the risk of misdiagnosis. Gutman said the process often requires some interpretation by a person's doctor.

"It's sort of the story, combined with MRI imaging, combined with other markers like spinal fluid, that help us make the MS diagnosis," Gutman said. "It's not like diabetes, where there's one blood test and if it's above this number, it's diabetes, if it's below this number, it isn't. There's a lot of things going into the diagnosis."

"Here comes something different"

Amerson had sometimes wondered if she was on the right medication for her MS, but she had never thought she might not have the condition. It had been a part of her life for so long that she took it as a fact. But a second opinion confirmed she had a rare condition called neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, or NMOSD.

Dr. Mark Tullman, associate director of the White Plains Hospital MS Center, described NMOSD as a rare autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system, especially the spinal cord and the optic nerves that connect the eyes and brain. Tullman, who did not treat Amerson, said the condition can cause similar symptoms to MS, including sudden vision loss, muscle weakness, bowel and bladder problems and loss of sensation. NMOSD symptoms tend to be more severe than those caused by MS, he said.

While MS has no single diagnostic test, many people with NMOSD have a detectable antibody in their blood, Tullman said. When a physician specifically looks for the presence or absence of that antibody, as the emergency room doctor Amerson had seen had, it can help inform an NMOSD diagnosis.

DeMonica Amerson. Erika Dufour/Amgen

When Amerson was told she didn't have MS, she was "so mad that (she) walked out" of the doctor's office.

"I had been dealing with this since I was 21 years old, and now, almost 20 years later, here comes something different," Amerson recalled thinking. "I didn't know there was another disease that mimics MS at all."

But Amerson knew she couldn't focus on the negative.

"I was mad. I don't want to say I got over it, but I accepted it," she said. "I said, 'I have to move forward. What does that look like?'"

"I choose to keep going forward"

Moving forward started with finding a new treatment option. Amerson, now 46, receives an infusion called Uplizna, which she said is "working well." She still experiences fatigue and pain. But she tries to take it "day by day."

Amerson said her "heart went out" to Applegate after hearing about the actor's misdiagnosis.

"I understand what it means to live in the unknown... I'm glad she went public with where she is and what she's going through," Amerson said.

DeMonica Amerson with her daughter and husband. DeMonica Amerson

Applegate's candor echoed Amerson's own focus on advocacy. Amerson said raising awareness for NMOSD has become a new passion. She hopes her advocacy efforts and emphasis on positivity will inspire her own daughters.

"We have so many people watching us. I know my girls are watching me. I have other teachers and leaders are watching. And so not only for them, but because I deserve the best version of myself that I can give," Amerson said. "I choose not to give up. I choose not to quit. I choose to keep going forward."

The National Weather Service says heavy rains are expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest

Heavy rains expected to bring flooding risk to already saturated parts of the US Southwest

Heavy rains starting Saturday evening were expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest through Monday, according to the National Weather Service.

As much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, where a number of weather systems have brought a deadly autumn of soaking rains. Several people were rescued from floodwaters Friday in Arizona and Nevada.

“It’s not going to take much rainfall to be impactful at all in some of these locations just because of how saturated they are,” said Allison Santorelli, a meteorologist with the Weather Prediction Center in College Park, Maryland.

The National Weather Service has issued flood watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. Those watches include the Four Corners region, a sparsely populated area where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet that has been hit especially hard by recent rains.

Santorelli said this weekend's rain was expected to bring both flash flooding and small-stream flooding.

The Phoenix Fire Department said in a post on X that it rescued people from four vehicles on flooded streets on Friday night, while a fire captain in nearby Scottsdale said on Facebook that crews were rescuing a person in one vehicle on a flooded street when another vehicle carrying two people drove into the same waters and had to be rescued.

Scottsdale fire Capt. Dave Folio said in a video posted on Facebook that just 2 inches (5 centimeters) of water can "sweep your vehicle off its wheels,'' and that the vehicles were in 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 meters) of water.

Crews in Henderson, Nevada, conducted three swift-water rescues during a downpour in the city just outside of Las Vegas on Friday afternoon, a city spokesperson told media outlets. One person was rescued from the top of their vehicle after it became stuck in floodwaters, two people were rescued from a vehicle swept from the roadway by floodwaters, and a person in a wash was rescued but then went into cardiac arrest and died at a hospital.

In western Arizona, heavy rains on Friday in Bullhead City left water, rocks and debris on streets across the city and closed parks, the city said in Facebook posts.

https://www.cbsnews.com/news/spirit-hall.text:
Shootings on Friday night in California and Michigan at Halloween Spirit stores, a retailer selling costumes and decor, killed two people, authorities said.

A shooting at a Halloween Spirit in Fairfield, California, killed one female and left six others wounded, police said. While at a Halloween Spirit in suburban Detroit, a shooting killed one male, police there said.

Constance Hages, a 31-year-old female, was killed in the California shooting, Fairfield Police said Saturday. Family members told detectives that Hages was pregnant at the time of her death.

Police said they are working to confirm that information following an examination by the Solano County Coroner.

Gunfire rang out inside Spirit Halloween, a store at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield late Friday, Fairfield police said in a statement posted on social media.

Fairfield Police said Saturday that, based on preliminary information, the shooting is believed to be a targeted incident involving one suspect inside the store. Detectives are continuing to actively investigate, police said.

All seven victims had gunshot wounds, including the person who died, the statement said. The remaining victims were taken to hospitals for treatment, and at least three people were in critical condition. The three victims in critical condition are a 16-year-old male, a 19-year-old male, and a 32-year-old male, police said. Another victim, a 23-year-old male, is also hospitalized in critical but stable condition. Two victims, a 19-year-old male and a 43-year-old male, were treated for their gunshot wounds and released from the hospital.

The statement posted around midnight early Saturday said that detectives were investigating and speaking with witnesses to try to identify a suspect.

"This is still a very active crime scene. Detectives are speaking with witnesses and diligently working to identify the suspect responsible for this horrific shooting," the statement said.

Fairfield is about 37 miles northeast of Sacramento.

Police in Madison Heights, Michigan, reported a shooting at a Halloween Spirit late Friday afternoon in which a 21-year-old man was killed. CBS News Detroit reports the suspected shooter, also age 21, was assaulted by the victim's family members and hospitalized with injuries. Police said the two men were acquainted and got in an altercation when the suspect shot the victim multiple times.

Madison Heights is located about 12 miles north of Detroit.

The affected Spirit Halloween stores will remain closed until the end of the season, a spokesperson for the company told CBS News in a statement on Saturday.

"We are deeply saddened by the tragic incidents that occurred at our Spirit Halloween stores. We extend our condolences to the families and individuals whose lives have been altered by these terrible events," the spokesperson said.
